That book by Jules Henry is titled "Culture Against" this figure. Essays on "The Sins of Legislators," "The Great Political Superstition," "The Coming Slavery," and "The New Toryism" comprise a book predicting a growth in the reach of the British government, written by Herbert Spencer and titled this "Versus the State." what is this figure, whose "Organization" type was studied by William Whyte and whose "Descent" was studied by Charles Darwin?

This novel's author was inspired by a collegiate paper on the theme of the double in the works of Dostoyevsky to create scenes in which the protagonist sees herself grossly distorted in a mirror. That protagonist throws all of her clothing off the roof of a hotel, cries while a photo of her holding a paper rose is being taken, and becomes violently ill after eating spoiled crab at a luncheon. That character is disgusted after seeing disc jockey Lenny Shepherd dancing with Doreen. Told by Dr. Gordon to seek shock therapy, the protagonist is funded at the hospital of Dr. Nolan by Philomena Guinea and, after Joan Gilling kills herself, is dumped by the tubercular Buddy Willard. Name this novel which follows a magazine intern during the summer of the execution of the Rosenbergs, written about Esther Greenwood by Sylvia Plath.

One character in this novel gives free shelter to destitute Okies but lectures them on being responsible for their own poverty, while another character hangs a Vermeer painting in his elevator. After a doctor in this novel sedates a man in order to seduce his mistress, Peter Boone is wrongly blamed for the affair and is shot by the owner of a mountaintop castle. A grotesque man wearing the Order of the Garter is found hiding out in a basement in this novel; that character had advocated eating raw carp in the eighteenth century as the Earl of Gonister. The protagonist is an archivist working with the Hauberk papers on behalf of a Hollywood millionaire who loves Virginia Maunciple, Jo Stoyte. What is this novel, named after a line that precedes "Me only cruel immortality consumes" in Tennyson's "Tithonus," which follows Jeremy Pordage's discovery of the secret of eternal life and was written by Aldous Huxley?
After Many a Summer Dies the Swan

One part attacks Ernest Barker for support of what the author of this book dubs a "caste state." Its chief critique of another figure accuses that person of the belief that sociology is reducible to psychology, a fallacy this work refers to as "psychologism." It reverses Emile Durkheim's use of the term "organic" in one section, and Walter Kaufmann alleged in "The Hegel Myth and Its Method" that this work based part of its conclusions on an incomplete edition of Hegel. Its first portion is titled for the "spell" of a figure whom the author accuses of perverting the intent of his teacher and of inspiring contemporary Fascists. It attacks Plato in an attempt to find the roots of the systems described in its author's previous work, The Poverty of Historicism. Name this defense of liberal democracy against the titular foes, a work of political philosophy by Karl Popper which lends its name to an "Institute" founded by Popper's disciple George Soros.
The Open Society and its Enemies

One of his plays includes the prophet Zizi and opens with an omniscient disembodied voice going over the entire plot, as well as including Anubis as the master of the Sphinx despite the subject matter being the Greek myth of Laius, Jocasta, and Oedipus. This author of such novels as The White Paper and Thomas the Imposter wrote more plays besides the aforementioned The Infernal Machine; for example, Michael is killed shortly after marrying Elizabeth in a play involving "The Room" and "The Game," fantasies inhabited by the childish Paul. In another play, an ominous horse spells out the French word "MERDE," meaning "Madame Eurydice will return from hell." name this frequent collaborator with Les Six, the author of Les Enfants Terribles and Orpheus.

The protagonist of this story punches a farmer of Crequetot in the stomach just before being mocked by a horse-dealer, even though he thought himself vindicated when Marius Paumelle made a discovery. The town crier interrupts lunch at Jordain's tavern to declare that Houlbreque has encountered misfortune, leading to the protagonist being accused of stealing from that man. The main character ultimately dies from his loss of reputation, even though the pocketbook in question turned up on the road. The vindictive harness-maker Malandain had accused the main character of picking up the money during the market of Goderville, but he was actually retrieving the title inconsequential object. The suspicious peasants of Normandy drive Hauchecorne to death in what story by Guy de Maupassant?

In one play by this author, Graham Dodd objects to Jean's leftist politics and Archie Rice runs out of money and audiences. The hardworking clerk Jones and the sexually confused Maples are directed to be played by the same actor in his play about Shirley and Joy abandoning the lecherous lawyer Bill Maitland. In addition to The Entertainer and Inadmissible Evidence, this author wrote a historical play in which the main character condemns the Peasants War and marries Katherina von Bora, Luther, and a play in which Helena Charles connives to make the pregnant Allison leave with Colonel Redfern in order to move in on misanthropic English workingman Jimmy Porter. Name this author of Look Back in Anger, a leading member of the "Angry Young Men."

The prostitute Minnie is patronized by two generations of the central family in this work, including a man who finds gold hidden beneath the floorboards by his late mother, which he uses as a bribe to acquire certain signatures. A key seduction in this play happens in a room that had previously been sealed in honor of its dead former occupant, and leads to a party where one man dances for so long that the fiddler passes out. However, the resultant baby is smothered out of the belief that it is an obstacle to love by Abbie Putnam. Name this play about Peter, Simeon, and Eben's rivalry for the farm that was abandoned during the gold rush by Ephraim Cabot, written by Eugene O'Neill.

This author's chief work of nonfiction is a manifesto against foreign food and places based on his trip to Japan, entitled The Frigate Pallada, and he wrote about Pyotr Ivanovich showing Alexander Aduyev around a city in his novel A Common Story. In another novel by this author, the title character is maneuvered into falling for his landlady Agafya by the Eric Mukherjee of Russian literature, an aryl halide-loving schemer named Mukhoyarov. Nikolay Dobrolyubov wrote about the "ism" of that novel, and this man also wrote about Olga Ilyinsky marrying Andrey Stolz after the owner of a large but remote estate is fleeced by his bailiffs and gets no work from his valet Zakhar. Name this author who wrote about a man who rarely rises from his bed, the supremely lazy Oblomov.

The protagonist of this novel has an internal dialogue between the figures of "Q" and "A" after realizing that he hates poor people, and saves his friend from being charged with adultery by hiding in the bathroom of a hotel before attacking "spiritually married men" while hitchhiking. One character is described as writing good poetry in the Nassau Lit, Thomas Parke D'Invilliers, while the main character wins membership in the Cottage Club and is about to take over the editorship of a newspaper before he is disqualified due to low grades. Later, that character maintains an epistolary romance with a woman met during a vacation in Minneapolis, Isabelle Borge. Rosalind Connage and the suicidal Eleanor Borge are some of the other women whom the central Princeton student meets. Name this novel about Amory Blaine, written by F. Scott Fitzgerald.

One writer used this language for such poems as "The Iron Cow Must Sweat" and the stories collected in Catastrophes before renouncing it and publishing subsequent works in English such as The True Confessions of an Albino Terrorist. Such figures as Adam Small and Etienne Leroux participated in the Sestigers, a group writing in this language, which had opposite politics to its early poets such as Totius. The slave Galant kills a member of the central family and Ma Rose becomes the spokesman for native dignity in A Chain of Voices, a novel by the author of A Dry White Season who may be the foremost author in this language. Name this tongue of Breyten Breytenbach and Andre Brink, a Dutch-derived language which competes with English and Xhosa for prominence in South Africa.

He wrote one notable work of fiction, the novel Norwood: A Tale of Village Life in New England, but is more known for such nonfiction works as Evolution and Religion and the product of eight years working in Indianapolis, which led him to explain the special needs of frontier town preaching in his Seven Lectures to Young Men. He founded such periodicals as The Independent and The Christian Union, which expounded the moderate Congregationalism he learned at Lane Theological Seminary, a school founded by this man's father. A lawsuit by Theodore Tilton accused this man of adultery, starting his feud with Victoria Woodhull. Name this celebrity preacher of the 1800s, the son of theologian Lyman and half-sibling of the suffragist Isabella and the author of Dred and Uncle Tom's Cabin, Harriet.

He created a character who pads his ass in order to look more powerful and takes pride in having the best flower garden in Africa, Mr. Blankensee, in a play about Kadidja starting a rebellion that the unattractive Leila and the traitor Said get involved in. One of his novels recalls Harcamone achieving godhood by killing a prison guard and Bulkaen being a divine instrument as well as a prison lover, after the protagonist is given life for stabbing a child in the eye. In addition to The Screens and The Miracle of the Rose, he wrote about The Bishop and The Chief of Police patronizing Irma at the title brothel, Salonge poisoning Clare instead of their employer, and Archibald Absalon Wellington arranging a stereotyped performance by the title racial group. Name this French playwright of The Balcony, The Maids, and The Blacks.

The narrator of this work hears birds performing polyphonic chanting after meeting the figure of Idelness, then sees a maiden at the Fountain of Narcissus. This poem in octasyllabic couplets opens by citing Macrobius's tale about Scipio to defend the veracity of dreams, and its last four fifths are a dialogue between the main characters on political topics. Inspired by Ovid's Art of Love and the chivalric writings of Andreas Capellanus, this poem was attacked by Christine de Pizan for its misogyny and was translated into Middle English in a mostly lost work of Geoffrey Chaucer. Name this work by Guillaume de Lorris and Jean de Meun about a garden of "fin d'amour."

One of this author's title characters is introduced by Colonel Hepburn to Gustavus Adolphus, while another is talked out of killing himself by the Quaker ship's surgeon Walter Waters. In addition to Memoirs of a Cavalier and Captain Singleton, he created a character who falls out with her maid Amy, Roxana, and the saddlemaking narrator H.F., who integrates his memories with tables of weekly death figures. Another of his books ends with the title character reuniting with Jeremy E. And repenting for such deeds as being a "transported felon in Virginia" and married to her own brother. He also wrote a novel based on the life of Alexander Selkirk featuring the native Friday. Name this writer of Journal of the Plague Year, Moll Flanders, and Robinson Crusoe.

One character in this work is imprisoned in an undersea dungeon after his attempt to kill his foes on the "stair of Merlin" is thwarted, and the title character becomes thirty-seventh in a certain ranking after drawing lots. A man who later becomes so excited at finding a magic spear that he starts killing everyone he sees, Astolpho, is given the first turn in a jousting contest against a man who can become invincible by placing a ring in his mouth, Uberto. The magician Malagigi unmasks one character in this work as the son of King Galaphron, Argalia, and its last sections deal with a siege of Paris by Agramant, the king of Africa. Agrican competes with the owner of Durindana for the hand of a princess of Cathay, Angelica, in, what work by Matteo Boiardo, an Italian epic about a paladin of Charlemagne which was followed by a Ludovico Ariosto work that finds the same character "angry?"

James Rockwell's son is saved from drowning in the last scene of this book, while one of the first scenes in this novel features a boy looking through the window of a restaurant at those who can afford breakfast. In addition to Johnny Nolan, its characters include an educated laborer who pays his rent by teaching his landlord how to read. The main character immediately figures out that Jim Travis is responsible after being robbed, and dubs himself a "capitalist" after he opens a bank account with the five dollars received for protecting the country rube Frank Whitney during an excursion to New York. Followed by the sequel Fame and Fortune, this novel was also the template for its author's similar works Paul the Peddler and Mark the Match- Boy. Name this story of bootblack Richard Hunter, who pluckishly works his way up to success, written by Horatio Alger.

Some episodes from this work's middle volume include the robbery of the shepherd Gros-Louis and a man whose job as an art critic is cut short on its first day by a military occupation. The character Birnenschatz tries to prove that he has no Jewish loyalties in this work, and the author's associate Paul Nizan is the model for the character Scheider, whom Brunet attempts to recruit to a militia in a prison camp. Lola Montero overdoes on cocaine after being asked for money by Boris, and Daniel Sereno lies about how much money he has after a doctor recommended by Sarah Gomez turns out to cost four thousand francs, when money for a proposed abortion by Marcelle is sought by the protagonist of its first volume, Mathieu Delarue. Including The Reprieve, Iron in the Soul, and The Age of Reason, name this cycle of novels taking place around the outbreak of World War II, by Jean-Paul Sartre.

The name of one character created by this author was used as a pseudonym by Charles P. Jacobs in a letter accusing Thomas Hardy of plagiarism. That character is introduced as a half-drowned body being carried into the Black Lion Inn. In addition to Timothy Crabshaw, this author wrote of a figure who tries to seduce Monimia by throwing Count Melvil under the bus, and about Tom Bowling's service on the HMS Thunder. This author of Launcelot Greaves and Ferdinand, Count Fathom wrote a novel in which Thomas Pipes is sent by Commodore Trunion to help a man who eventually marries Emilia Gauntlet, and another Lydia Melford and Letitia Lewis carry on a similar friendship through letters as Dr. Richard Lewis does with Matthew Bramble. Name this author of Peregrine Pickle, Roderick Random, and Humphrey Clinker.

This work ends after the protagonist becomes agitated and knocks over a vase of water at a restaurant while catching sight of a gangster eating nearby. During his childhood, that character passes out and is presumed dead on a monthly basis, and comes back to life by wetting himself. The protagonist believes that seeing a harvester of human fertilizer at work in tight pants was an important moment in his life and is disappointed to find out that a picture of an armored knight is really Joan of Arc. This novel ends with the final breakup between a man who used to dress up as Cleopatra and the perceptive Sonoko, who understands why the narrator rarely kisses her. After faking an illness to avoid the draft, the protagonist hopes to die in an American air raid, ending the crisis which began when he masturbated to a painting by Guido Reni of the martyrdom of Saint Sebastian and realized that he was in love with the tough schoolmate Omi. Name this mostly autobiographical novel about Kochan, a closet homosexual in upper-class Japan, written by Yukio Mishima.
